6.3a — Jump Feel: Fall Speed & Coyote Time

Your jump works (6.2a) but it feels like a spreadsheet. Nobody can say WHY — until you learn that "feel" is three tunables with names: asymmetric gravity, jump buffer, and coyote time. Today you make a jump that players call "tight" without knowing they were taught to.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Feel rule #1 — fall faster than you rise. Real games multiply gravity while falling. New code, same voice:

[SerializeField] private float fallMultiplier = 2.5f;

private void FixedUpdate()
{
    if (isPlatformer && rb.velocity.y < 0)
    {
        // falling: pull harder
        rb.gravityScale = baseGravity * fallMultiplier;
    }
    else if (rb.velocity.y > 0)
    {
        rb.gravityScale = baseGravity; // rising: normal
    }
}

Save baseGravity in Start (read rb.gravityScale once). Now rise is a balloon and fall is a decision. Try it with fallMultiplier 1: the floaty "moon hop" you tuned away by hand in 6.1a — this one knob replaces three fiddly jumpForce settings, and it is why nearly every platformer you love does NOT obey real physics.

Feel rule #2 — forgive the player. Two classic mercies, both timers (the 3.3a pattern, pointed at kindness):

NameThe complaint it killsImplementation
Coyote time"I jumped but the ledge ate it"remember the last grounded moment; allow jump for ~0.1s after
Jump buffer"I pressed too early, nothing happened"remember the last Space press; fire the jump the instant you land

Socratic

Both mercies are the SAME pattern: remember an event's timestamp, compare against Time.time, act on the gap. Why does this NOT make the game easier — what is the difference between forgiving the player's intent and playing for them?

Build Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — coyote time. Two fields and one comparison, added to the ground check from 6.2a:

[SerializeField] private float coyoteTime = 0.1f;
private float lastGroundedTime;

// inside Update, right after isGrounded is set:
if (isGrounded) lastGroundedTime = Time.time;

// and the jump condition becomes:
if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)
    && Time.time - lastGroundedTime <= coyoteTime)
{
    rb.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    lastGroundedTime = -999f; // spend the coyote
}

Test the exact way players fail: run off a ledge and tap Space a beat late — you jump! Set coyoteTime to 0: the complaint is back. Set it to 0.5: you can fly off ledges for half a second — tune until the mercy is invisible.

Step 2 — jump buffer. The mirror image: remember when the key was pressed, allow the jump shortly after landing:

[SerializeField] private float jumpBuffer = 0.12f;
private float lastJumpPressTime;

if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)) lastJumpPressTime = Time.time;

if (isGrounded && Time.time - lastJumpPressTime <= jumpBuffer)
{
    rb.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    lastJumpPressTime = -999f;
}

Test: stand under a low ceiling... no — simpler: press Space a hair before you land from a jump. Before the buffer: nothing, press again. After: the jump just HAPPENS. Your inputs feel honored.

Bug Hunt: The mushy jump

  1. Forget to spend the coyote (no lastGroundedTime = -999 after the jump). Jump once in place, repeatedly. What does Time.time - lastGroundedTime equal while you are STILL on the ground — and why does that mean the mercy never expires?
  2. Coyote time lets you jump from a SPIKE's edge after you already left ground. Trace lastGroundedTime through the death (2.2a) — why does respawn reset the mercy, and should it?
  3. Buffer 0.12 with a LOW jump means double-fire chains: land → buffer fires → land again... how would the -999 spend stop this on the SECOND landing?
  4. Set fallMultiplier to 10. The character lands like a dropped anvil — fun? For which genre would 10 be correct (one-word answer: a ___ game like Downwell)?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Feel portfolio

  1. Tune a "heavy knight": fallMultiplier 3, coyote 0.08, buffer 0.08. Then a "nimble rogue": 1.8, 0.15, 0.2. Swap a partner between yours and theirs — can they feel the class you built without being told?
  2. Write your three numbers on paper and hand them to another team — rebuild from paper only. Are the numbers a program? (AP exam word: abstraction — what do the numbers HIDE?)
  3. Commit + push: "6.3a: fall multiplier + coyote + buffer".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain asymmetric gravity and wire fallMultiplier in FixedUpdate
  • Build coyote time and jump buffer from the timestamp pattern
  • Explain "spending" a grace period and what double-fire is
  • Defend mercies as intent-forgiveness, not difficulty-lowering
